subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Look around you for a moment. If you are sitting near a window, you might see a acacia tree waving in the wind, a lizard sunning itself on a warm rock, a goat chewing, or a flamingo wading in a shallow lake. You might also see stones, a plastic bottle, a metal spoon and the phone or tablet you are learning from. Some of these things are alive and some have never been alive. In this unit you will learn how scientists tell the difference, and then how they sort the enormous variety of living things into neat, useful groups.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Describe the seven characteristics of living organisms.
Discuss reasons for classifying viruses as living or non-living.
Describe a species as a group of organisms that can reproduce to produce fertile offspring.
Use and construct dichotomous keys to classify species and groups of related organisms.
Sort, group and classify phenomena, objects, materials and organisms through testing, observation, using secondary information, and making and using keys.

outcomes: By the end of this unit, you will be able to:
List and describe the seven characteristics shared by all living organisms.
Decide whether an object is living, non-living, or was once alive, giving reasons.
Describe the main groups (kingdoms) into which living things are classified.
Explain the difference between vertebrates and invertebrates and give local examples of each.
Describe the structure of a virus and discuss why scientists argue about whether viruses are alive.
Define the word 'species' and explain how scientists decide if two organisms belong to the same species.
Use a dichotomous key to identify an organism, working through it step by step.
Construct your own dichotomous key to identify a small set of local animals, leaves or objects.
Study this table before you read on. These words appear again and again throughout the unit, so learning them early will make everything easier.

concepts.title: Sorting Life Into Big Groups: The Kingdoms
concepts.explanation:
Once we agree that something is alive, the next question is: what kind of living thing is it? To answer this, biologists sort all organisms into a few very large groups called kingdoms. Think of a kingdom as the biggest box on the shelf. Inside each big box are smaller boxes, and inside those are smaller boxes still, until finally we reach a single species. Sorting life into groups like this is called classification.

Scientists have used different numbers of kingdoms over the years. A simple and common system uses five kingdoms. Some newer systems split these further into six or seven groups, but the five-kingdom idea is a clear place to start.

Many cells; cannot make their own food, so must eat other organisms; usually move about.

Lions, camels, flamingos, tilapia, beetles, humans.

Many cells; make their own food by photosynthesis using sunlight; usually green; do not move about.

Made of cells with walls but no chlorophyll; feed on dead or living material; reproduce by spores.

Mostly single-celled; a mixed group; some are like tiny animals, some like tiny plants.

Amoeba; the parasite that causes malaria; many pond algae.

Single-celled and very tiny; have cell walls but no nucleus; found almost everywhere.

The bacteria in soil, in yoghurt and camel milk, and some that cause disease.

Notice how the kingdoms are separated by big, clear differences: whether an organism makes its own food or eats others, whether it is made of one cell or many, and whether its cells have a nucleus. These same 'either/or' differences are exactly the kind of questions we will use later to build identification keys.

It helps to think of classification as a set of boxes inside boxes, getting smaller as you go in. The kingdom is the biggest box. Inside a kingdom, organisms are sorted into a phylum, then into a class, and on through smaller and smaller groups until you reach a single species. You do not need to memorise every level in Year 7, but it is worth knowing the idea: a camel and a lion share the same kingdom (animals) and even the same class (mammals), but they part ways lower down, ending in two different species. The closer two organisms sit in this system of boxes, the more features they share. This is why a camel is far more like a goat than either is like an acacia tree.

The animal kingdom is huge, so biologists split it in two using a single important feature: the backbone, also called the spine. Run your fingers down the middle of your back and you will feel a line of small bones — that is your backbone. Animals with a backbone are called vertebrates. Animals without a backbone are called invertebrates.

The vertebrates are divided into five familiar classes. Fish (such as tilapia and Nile perch) live in water and breathe using gills. Amphibians (such as frogs) live partly in water and partly on land. Reptiles (such as lizards, snakes and crocodiles) have dry, scaly skin. Birds (such as flamingos, ostriches and chickens) have feathers and wings. Mammals (such as camels, lions, elephants and humans) have hair or fur and feed their young on milk.

Even though vertebrates are the animals we notice most easily, they are actually the minority. The great majority of animals on Earth — well over nine out of every ten known species — are invertebrates. These include insects (beetles, mosquitoes, bees, grasshoppers), spiders and scorpions, crabs and prawns from the Indian Ocean coast, and worms and snails from the soil. The mosquito that spreads malaria is an invertebrate, which is why classifying and understanding insects can be a matter of life and health.

One quick trick to tell an insect from a spider — two invertebrates people often mix up — is to count the legs. An insect always has six legs and its body is in three parts; a spider has eight legs and its body is in two parts. So the beetle Khadija finds on the windowsill is an insect, but the small creature spinning a web in the corner is a spider. This single 'six legs or eight legs?' question is a perfect example of the clear, either-or thinking you will use when you build a key later in this unit. Careful counting beats guessing every time.

Did You Know? There are more kinds of beetle than any other type of animal on Earth — well over 350,000 described species, with more found every year. If you gathered every animal species and picked one at random, there is a good chance it would be a beetle.

Some things sit right on the border between living and non-living, and the most famous example is the virus. Viruses are the cause of illnesses you will know well: the common cold, influenza (flu), measles, and COVID-19, which is caused by a virus called SARS-CoV-2.

Viruses are astonishingly small — far smaller than one of your own cells. You cannot see a virus with an ordinary school microscope, no matter how good it is. To see one, scientists use a special and very powerful instrument called an electron microscope, which uses beams of electrons instead of light. In photographs from an electron microscope, viruses are shown magnified around 100,000 times, and even then they look tiny.

A virus has a very simple structure. On the outside is a coat made of protein. Sticking out of this coat are little pegs or spikes. Inside the coat is the virus's set of instructions, written in genetic material such as RNA. That is almost all there is to a virus: instructions wrapped in a protein coat. A virus is not made of cells. It has no cell membrane, no cytoplasm and no nucleus.

Here is the crucial point. On its own, a virus can do nothing at all. It does not respire, does not feed, does not grow, does not excrete, is not sensitive and cannot move. It is only when a virus gets inside a living cell that anything happens. The spikes on the coat let the virus stick to one of your cells and slip inside. Once in, the virus forces your cell to read its instructions and build many new copies of the virus. This copying is called replication. The new viruses then burst out, usually killing the cell, and spread to infect more cells. That is what makes you feel ill.

Did You Know? The H3N2 influenza virus that spread around the world in 1968 and 1969 caused a flu pandemic that is thought to have killed around one million people. A particle far too small to see with a school microscope changed the lives of millions — a powerful reminder of why hygiene matters.

So, are viruses alive? Scientists genuinely disagree. On one hand, a virus can reproduce (replicate) and it has genetic instructions, just like living things. On the other hand, it shows none of the other characteristics of life on its own — it cannot respire, feed, grow, excrete, sense or move without hijacking a living cell. For this reason, most biologists place viruses in a category of their own, on the borderline between living and non-living. There is no single 'correct' answer, and that is exactly what makes viruses such a fascinating puzzle.

Understanding viruses is also deeply practical. Because viruses spread from person to person, simple habits protect whole communities: washing your hands with soap and clean water, covering your mouth when you cough or sneeze, staying home when unwell, and taking vaccinations such as the measles vaccine. In Islam, cleanliness is greatly encouraged, and keeping yourself and your surroundings clean is one of the best defences against these invisible particles.

We have sorted life into kingdoms, and animals into vertebrates and invertebrates. But the smallest and most important group of all is the species. When you name a single kind of organism — a lion, a camel, an acacia tree — you are naming a species.

All the members of one species share the same basic characteristics, but they are not identical to one another. Some camels are taller, some are a lighter colour, some have longer eyelashes. These differences between members of the same species are called variation. Variation is completely normal — look around any classroom and you will see that all the students are human, yet no two are exactly alike.

Because of variation, it can be hard to decide whether two similar-looking organisms are the same species or two different species. Imagine two birds in your garden that look nearly the same. How can a scientist be sure? The clearest test is reproduction. Scientists define a species as a group of organisms that can reproduce together to produce fertile offspring.

The word fertile is the key. Fertile offspring are able to grow up and have young of their own. For example, the African elephant and the Indian elephant look similar but belong to two different species: they live in different places and normally do not reproduce together. By contrast, all camels can breed with one another and their calves can grow up and breed too, so all camels are one species.

Did You Know? Very rarely, a male lion and a female tiger kept together in a zoo produce a cub called a 'liger'. Ligers are healthy, but they are infertile — they cannot have young of their own. This is one of the strongest reasons scientists say lions and tigers are two different species, even though they can occasionally breed.

So when a scientist studies two kinds of parakeet and never once finds them making nests together in the wild, that is good evidence they are separate species. To be even more certain, the scientist would check many more pairs in the wild, because a single observation could be a coincidence. Careful, repeated observation is what turns a guess into scientific evidence.
concepts.example: There is a neat way to remember the species idea. Members of the same species usually look similar to one another, and look different from members of other species. But looks alone are not enough, because variation can make two members of one species look quite different, while two separate species can look almost the same. The reliable test is always reproduction: can they breed together and produce young that can, in turn, breed? For example, a donkey and a horse can produce a mule, but the mule is infertile — so donkeys and horses are two different species, just like lions and tigers. This is why scientists treat the 'fertile offspring' rule as the final word.

concepts.title: Identifying Organisms With Keys
concepts.explanation:
Suppose Amina finds an insect near Hargeisa that she has never seen before, and she wants to know its name. She could look through pictures in a book or on the internet and hope to spot a match — but with millions of species, that could take a very long time. Biologists have a much smarter tool: a key.

A key is a set of questions or statements about an organism. Each answer sends you to the next question, and you keep going until you arrive at the organism's name. The most common type is a dichotomous key. The word dichotomous means 'branching into two', because at every step you choose between exactly two options — yes or no, this or that.

A key can be written in two styles. The first style uses branching questions. You start at the top and follow the branches. For example, a simple key to sort five small animals — a crab, an earthworm, a housefly, a dragonfly and a slug — might work like this:

Does it have legs? If NO, ask: is its body made of rings? If yes it is an earthworm; if no it is a slug.

If it DOES have legs, ask: does it have more than six legs? If yes it is a crab.

If it has exactly six legs, ask: does it have four wings? If yes it is a dragonfly; if no it is a housefly.

The second style uses numbered pairs of statements. Instead of a picture with branches, you read a pair of statements, choose the one that fits, and it tells you which number to go to next. Here is exactly the same key written in the numbered style:

Both styles contain exactly the same information — they are just laid out differently. Many people find the numbered style easier because you never lose your place. Being able to change a key from one style to the other is a useful scientific skill.

Keys are used for far more than small animals. Scientists have keys to identify fish, birds, leaves, flowers, seeds and even bacteria grown in a laboratory. A fisherman on the Indian Ocean coast could use a key to name a fish by asking whether it has stripes, whether the stripes are vertical, and whether its fins have spines. A farmer could use a key to name a weed growing in the maize. Whatever the organism, the method is always the same: start at the top, answer one clear question at a time, and let each answer carry you closer to a single name. The power of a key is that it turns a hard problem — 'what on earth is this?' — into a short series of easy choices.

Worked Example: Using the Key Step by Step

Let us identify the dragonfly using the numbered key above. We will show every step so you can see exactly how a key is used. Imagine you are holding the whole animal and can look at it carefully.

Start at step 1. Look at the dragonfly. Does it have legs? Yes. Statement 1a says 'It has legs — go to 2.' So we go to step 2.

Step 2. Does it have exactly six legs? Yes, like all insects it has six legs. Statement 2a says 'It has exactly six legs — go to 4.' So we go to step 4.

Step 4. Does it have four wings? Yes, a dragonfly has four wings. Statement 4a says 'It has four wings — dragonfly.'

We have arrived at the answer: dragonfly. The path we followed was 1a, 2a, 4a.
concepts.example: Now try the earthworm yourself before reading on. Start at step 1. An earthworm has no legs, so statement 1b sends you to step 3. At step 3, an earthworm's body is made of rings, so statement 3a gives the answer: earthworm. The path was 1b, 3a. Notice that you never needed steps 2 or 4 — a good key lets you reach an answer in as few steps as possible.

concepts.title: Building Your Own Key
concepts.explanation:
Using a key is one skill; making one is the real test of understanding. Suppose you want a key to tell apart four different leaves you collected from your compound — say an acacia leaf, a mango leaf, a maize leaf and an aloe vera leaf. Here is the method:

Lay out all four specimens and look for one feature that splits them into two groups. For example, 'Is the leaf long and narrow?' might put maize and aloe in one group, and acacia and mango in the other.

Take one group and find a feature that separates it into two. For example, among the long narrow leaves: 'Is the leaf thick and fleshy?' separates aloe vera (yes) from maize (no).

Repeat for the other group until every specimen is identified on its own.

Write your steps as numbered pairs, each ending either in another step or in the name of a leaf.

A good key follows two golden rules. First, every question must have a clear yes-or-no answer that anyone would agree on. 'Does the leaf have a smooth edge?' is a good question. 'Is the leaf pretty?' or 'Is the plant tall?' are bad questions, because different people will answer them differently — one person's 'tall' is another person's 'short'. Second, keep your key short: for four organisms you should need only three pairs of statements.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Conservationists in East Africa use keys and careful classification to decide which animals are separate, endangered species that need protecting. Sometimes scientists disagree about whether two similar animals are one species or two — and that disagreement can decide whether a whole forest or habitat is saved. Classification is not just naming; it can protect creation.

concepts.title: Guided Exploration
concepts.explanation:
Work through these questions in your notebook. They are designed to build your understanding step by step, so think carefully before you write.

A flame moves, gives out heat, seems to grow, and uses oxygen. Which characteristics of life does it appear to show? Which important ones does it clearly lack? Is it alive?

A date seed is dry and still for years, then grows into a palm when planted. Was the seed alive while it was resting? Explain your thinking.

Sort these into vertebrate or invertebrate: tilapia, mosquito, camel, scorpion, ostrich, garden snail.

Explain in your own words why a virus is hard to place on the living/non-living scale.

Two goats in a herd look slightly different from each other. Are they different species? Explain using the word variation.

Why is 'Is the animal big?' a poor question to use in a dichotomous key? Suggest a better one.

concepts.title: Passage: Halima's Beetle
concepts.explanation: One warm afternoon in Garissa, Halima was helping her grandmother sort dried beans when a shiny black beetle scuttled across the mat. 'What is it?' she asked. Her older brother Yusuf, who was studying science, smiled. 'Let us find out like a scientist,' he said. 'First, is it alive?' Halima watched it move, saw it sense her shadow and dart away, and remembered it must also feed, grow, respire, excrete and one day reproduce. 'Yes,' she said, 'it shows all seven signs of life.' Yusuf nodded. 'Good. Now, does it have a backbone?' Halima thought. 'No — it has a hard shell on the outside instead. So it is an invertebrate, an insect.' Yusuf then drew a small key on paper: does it have wings, how many legs, what colour. Working through it together, they gave the beetle a name. 'You see,' Yusuf said, 'you did not need a book of a million pictures. You only needed careful questions, one at a time.' Halima grinned, already planning a key for every insect in the compound.
concepts.example: Say this idea back in your own words: One warm afternoon in Garissa, Halima was helping her grandmother sort dried beans when a shiny black beetle scuttled across the mat. Then find one example of passage: halima's beetle around your home or outside.

methods.title: Living, Non-living or Once-living?
methods.example: To sort objects from around your home into three groups — living, non-living, and once-living — using the seven characteristics of life.
steps: Draw a table with three columns: Living, Non-living (never alive), and Once-living.
Take each object in turn. Ask: does it show all seven signs of life right now?
If it shows all seven, place it in Living. If it never had life, place it in Non-living.
If it does not show the signs now but was once part of a living thing (like wood or cloth), place it in Once-living.
For each object, write one reason for your choice.

methods.title: A Leaf Hunt and Sorting Challenge
methods.example: To collect several different leaves from around your home and sort them into groups based on features you can observe — the first step towards building a key.
steps: Lay all your leaves side by side on a clean surface.
Choose one feature — for example, 'Is the leaf long and narrow?' — and split the leaves into two piles: yes and no.
For each pile, choose another feature and split again.
Keep going until every leaf is separated from all the others.
Record which feature you used at each split.

methods.title: Build Your Own Dichotomous Key
methods.example: To construct a working dichotomous key that another person can use to identify four local insects or four leaves.
steps: Observe all four specimens carefully and list the features of each (number of legs, wings, size, colour, body shape).
Find one feature that splits the four into two groups of two. Write it as statement 1a and 1b.
For each group of two, find a feature that separates them. Write these as statements 2 and 3.
Each statement must end either in 'go to ...' or in the name of the organism.
Write your finished key neatly using numbered pairs.

methods.title: Modelling a Virus
methods.example: To make a simple model of a virus so you can understand and remember its structure.
steps: Form the dough or paper into a round ball. This is the protein coat.
Before closing the ball, tuck a few short threads inside. These are the RNA instructions.
Push the toothpicks or twigs gently into the outside of the ball to make the spikes.
Look at your model. Label a drawing of it in your notebook: protein coat, RNA, spikes.

workedExamples.title: Using the Key Step by Step
workedExamples.prompt: Let us identify the dragonfly using the numbered key above. We will show every step so you can see exactly how a key is used. Imagine you are holding the whole animal and can look at it carefully.
workedExamples.solution:
Start at step 1. Look at the dragonfly. Does it have legs? Yes. Statement 1a says 'It has legs — go to 2.' So we go to step 2.

Step 2. Does it have exactly six legs? Yes, like all insects it has six legs. Statement 2a says 'It has exactly six legs — go to 4.' So we go to step 4.

Step 4. Does it have four wings? Yes, a dragonfly has four wings. Statement 4a says 'It has four wings — dragonfly.'

We have arrived at the answer: dragonfly. The path we followed was 1a, 2a, 4a.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 3
workedExamples.prompt: Breaking down food inside cells to release energy is called: (a) excretion (b) respiration (c) nutrition (d) growth
workedExamples.solution: (b) respiration. Respiration releases energy from food inside every cell.

workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is an invertebrate? (a) tilapia (b) camel (c) mosquito (d) flamingo

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: Getting rid of waste made inside the body is called: (a) nutrition (b) sensitivity (c) excretion (d) reproduction
workedExamples.solution: (c) excretion. Excretion is removing waste made inside the body, such as carbon dioxide.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: Which instrument is needed to see a virus? (a) a hand lens (b) a school light microscope (c) an electron microscope (d) a telescope
workedExamples.solution: (c) an electron microscope. Viruses are far too small for a school light microscope.

activities.title: Living, Non-living or Once-living?
activities.materials: A notebook and pencil; About ten safe objects you can gather: a stone, a plastic cup, a metal spoon, a wooden spoon, a piece of cloth, a leaf, a potted plant, a piece of dried date, a feather, a small potted seedling
steps: Draw a table with three columns: Living, Non-living (never alive), and Once-living.
Take each object in turn. Ask: does it show all seven signs of life right now?
If it shows all seven, place it in Living. If it never had life, place it in Non-living.
If it does not show the signs now but was once part of a living thing (like wood or cloth), place it in Once-living.
For each object, write one reason for your choice.

activities.title: A Leaf Hunt and Sorting Challenge
activities.materials: Four to six different leaves you can safely pick or find fallen (for example acacia, mango, maize, aloe vera, grass, a flowering shrub); A notebook, pencil and a ruler
steps: Lay all your leaves side by side on a clean surface.
Choose one feature — for example, 'Is the leaf long and narrow?' — and split the leaves into two piles: yes and no.
For each pile, choose another feature and split again.
Keep going until every leaf is separated from all the others.
Record which feature you used at each split.

activities.title: Build Your Own Dichotomous Key
activities.materials: Four different specimens: either four insects you have observed (housefly, ant, beetle, grasshopper) or four leaves from Investigation 2; Notebook and pencil
steps: Observe all four specimens carefully and list the features of each (number of legs, wings, size, colour, body shape).
Find one feature that splits the four into two groups of two. Write it as statement 1a and 1b.
For each group of two, find a feature that separates them. Write these as statements 2 and 3.
Each statement must end either in 'go to ...' or in the name of the organism.
Write your finished key neatly using numbered pairs.

activities.title: Modelling a Virus
activities.materials: A ball of soft dough (flour and water) or clay, or a scrunched ball of paper; Small pieces of thread, wool or torn paper (to be the RNA inside); Toothpicks, matchsticks or small dry twigs (to be the spikes) — handle carefully; A small clear bag or bowl to hold the model
steps: Form the dough or paper into a round ball. This is the protein coat.
Before closing the ball, tuck a few short threads inside. These are the RNA instructions.
Push the toothpicks or twigs gently into the outside of the ball to make the spikes.
Look at your model. Label a drawing of it in your notebook: protein coat, RNA, spikes.

connections.text: Cells (Unit 1): all living things are made of cells — except viruses, which are not. This unit builds directly on what a cell is.
Food chains and ecology (later units): classifying organisms into producers, herbivores and carnivores depends on the grouping skills you learned here.
understanding viruses connects to real life — preventing measles, flu and COVID-19 through cleanliness and vaccination.
the kingdoms and species of East Africa link to habitats like the savanna, the Rift Valley lakes and the Indian Ocean coast.
building and reading keys uses clear logical thinking — the same 'if yes... if no...' reasoning used in problem solving.

realProblems.prompt: Amina finds a small creature with eight legs and no wings near her home in Hargeisa. Using the idea of a key, what question would help her decide if it is an insect or a spider? What is your reasoning?
realProblems.answer: A good question is 'Does it have six legs?' (or 'Does it have eight legs?'). Insects have six legs; spiders have eight. Since the creature has eight legs, it is a spider, not an insect.

realProblems.prompt: During a measles outbreak, Farah's little brother is unwell. Explain, using what you know about how viruses replicate, why keeping him at home and washing hands protects the rest of the family.
realProblems.answer: A virus can only make copies inside a living cell and spreads from person to person. Keeping the brother at home stops the virus reaching others, and washing hands removes particles before they spread. Together this breaks the chain of infection.

realProblems.prompt: A farmer near the Jubba River has two herds of cattle that look slightly different. How could he find out whether they are the same species?

reasoningPrompts.prompt: List the seven characteristics of living organisms.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition (MRS GREN). Each is a sign of life.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the difference between respiration and breathing.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Breathing is moving air in and out of the body. Respiration happens inside every cell, breaking down food to release energy. Plants respire but do not breathe.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Give one example each of a living, a non-living, and a once-living object from your home.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Answers vary. Example: living = a potted plant; non-living = a stone; once-living = a wooden spoon (it came from a tree).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between a vertebrate and an invertebrate? Give one local example of each.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A vertebrate has a backbone (e.g. tilapia or camel); an invertebrate has none (e.g. a mosquito or scorpion).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Describe the three main parts of a virus.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A virus has a protein coat on the outside, spikes/pegs sticking out of it, and RNA (genetic instructions) inside. It is not made of cells.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Define the word species in your own words.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A species is a group of organisms that share the same features and can reproduce together to produce fertile offspring.

rounds.explanation: mosquito. A mosquito has no backbone, so it is an invertebrate. The others are vertebrates.

rounds.prompt: Which instrument is needed to see a virus?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: an electron microscope. Viruses are far too small for a school light microscope.

games.title: Spot the Error: Nutrition
games.description: Practise nutrition through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: Which is the best question for a dichotomous key?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Does it have six legs? It has a clear yes-or-no answer everyone would agree on.

rounds.prompt: How many characteristics of life do all living organisms share?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: seven. All living things share the seven MRS GREN characteristics.

rounds.prompt: A virus's outer coat is made of:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: protein. The outer coat of a virus is made of protein, with spikes on it.

rounds.prompt: A group of organisms that can reproduce to make fertile offspring is a:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: species. A species is defined by the ability to produce fertile offspring together.

games.title: Mastery Mix: Kingdom
games.description: Practise kingdom through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: Green plants get their nutrition by:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: photosynthesis. Green plants make their own food using sunlight, water and air.

rounds.prompt: Breaking down food inside cells to release energy is called:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Respiration releases energy from food inside every cell.

rounds.prompt: Getting rid of waste made inside the body is called:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Excretion is removing waste made inside the body, such as carbon dioxide.

rounds.prompt: The offspring of a lion and a tiger (a liger) is:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: infertile. Ligers are healthy but cannot have young, so they are infertile.

games.title: Unit Champion: Vertebrate
games.description: Practise vertebrate through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: Which kingdom does a mushroom belong to?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: fungi. Mushrooms belong to the fungi kingdom; they do not photosynthesise.

rounds.prompt: Which instrument is needed to see a virus?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: an electron microscope. Viruses are far too small for a school light microscope.

rounds.prompt: 'Dichotomous' means:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: branching into two. At each step a dichotomous key offers exactly two choices.

selfAssessment: I can by the end of this unit, you will be able to:
I can list and describe the seven characteristics shared by all living organisms.
I can decide whether an object is living, non-living, or was once alive, giving reasons.
I can describe the main groups (kingdoms) into which living things are classified.
I can explain the difference between vertebrates and invertebrates and give local examples of each.
I can describe the structure of a virus and discuss why scientists argue about whether viruses are alive.
I can define the word 'species' and explain how scientists decide if two organisms belong to the same species.
I can use a dichotomous key to identify an organism, working through it step by step.
